generator.params.frond_length.why: A palm's leaf is its frond, petiole and all, drawn as long as its flora gives it.

generator.params.fan.why: A fan palm's frond ends in a fan of segments; a feather palm's bears leaflets along its rachis.

generator.params.petiole.why: A fan palm's blade stands at the end of a petiole about half the frond's length (the built-in cabbage, saw and fan palms, 0.45 to 0.54); a feather palm's leaflets start a short way up (date and royal palms, 0.1 to 0.22).

generator.params.pieces.why: A feather palm's rachis is drawn in many pieces to bear its leaflets; a fan palm's petiole needs few.

generator.params.old_angle.why: Fan palms' old fronds stand out flatter (the built-in fan palms, 72 to 75 degrees from the vertical) than feather palms' arching ones (55 to 62).

generator.params.hang.why: An old fan frond turns further down before it dies than a feather palm's (the built-in species, 35 to 50 against 20 to 25 degrees, short of the most, which hang in a skirt).

generator.params.fan_arch.why: A fan's edge segments droop below its middle, as the built-in cabbage and California fan palms' do (30 to 35 degrees).

appearance.organs.leaflet.bend.fold.why: A palm's leaflet is a fold of its pleated blade: V-shaped, trough up, where the blade split along its upper folds (induplicate), keeled where it split along its lower ones (reduplicate); a cycad's or a fern's is flat.

appearance.organs.ray.bend.fold.why: A fan's segments are folds of its pleated blade too, V-shaped where it split along its upper folds, keeled where along its lower.

generator.params.leaflet_scatter.why: A feather palm's leaflets stand a little above and below the rachis's V, not in two flat planes (the built-in date and royal palms, 15 to 18 degrees; less for most).

generator.params.suckers.why: A clonal palm (Tomlinson's model: stems from the foot of the first) sends up suckers round its foot; a solitary one sends none.

generator.params.petiole_radius.why: A longer frond stands on a stouter petiole and rachis: the built-in palms' are 0.008 to 0.01 of the frond's length in radius (saw palmetto 8 mm on a 1.25 m frond, royal palm 35 mm on 3.5 m).

generator.params.trunk_rate.why: A palm's crown stands about four tenths of a frond's length above its trunk, so its trunk rises to the rest of its usual height over about fifty years.

generator.params.split_depth.why: A fan's segments are free of each other only over the share of the blade its flora says it is divided; inside that the blade is one piece, the palman.

generator.params.tip_droop.why: Where its segments part, a stiff fan's go on in the blade's plane, a drooping fan's free parts bend down and a pendulous one's hang (degrees, set by eye from the floras' words); the segment's card bends on down along its length.

generator.params.filaments.why: A fan with a few threads bears one in every other sinus between its segments; one with many bears one in every sinus and two more along each segment's free margin, the last at its tip.

generator.params.tooth_length.why: An armed petiole's teeth as long as its flora gives them, else a few millimetres for fine teeth and about a centimetre and a half for stout ones (set by eye); an unarmed petiole has none.

generator.params.tooth_spacing.why: Teeth as far apart as the flora gives them, else about three of their lengths apart (set by eye).

generator.params.tooth_angle.why: A straight tooth stands square to the petiole; a curved one leans back toward the stem and a hooked one further (degrees from the way to the blade). A card is flat, so its curve is drawn as its lean.

generator.params.tooth_tip.why: Teeth that become smaller and sparser toward the blade end at about a third of their size near the petiole's foot (set by eye).

generator.params.pinna_pairs.why: A twice-pinnate frond's pinnae, in pairs along its rachis.

generator.params.pinna_leaflets.why: The leaflets on each pinna of a twice-pinnate frond: those each side of its rachis, with one more at its tip.

appearance.organs.tooth.colour.why: A petiole's teeth are drawn in the colour the flora gives them.

appearance.organs.dead.colour.why: A dead frond that stays on the stem is drawn in the colour the flora gives the dead leaves.

appearance.organs.pinnule.shape.praemors.why: A praemorse leaflet's broad tip is jagged, bitten into uneven teeth about a seventh of its length deep (set by eye).

appearance.organs.pinnule.shape.midrib.why: A leaflet without a midrib, whose main veins fan out from its base, is drawn with none.

generator.params.dead_fold_years.why: A palm's dead leaf that stays on the stem first stands out at its last living angle below the crown, then falls against the stem over about a year (set by eye from photographs of skirted fan palms), so the thatch meets the living crown.

generator.params.trunk_radius.why: A trunk's radius, a little under half its greatest stated diameter, since a palm's trunk is widest at its foot or its belly.

generator.defaults.trunk_radius.why: Where no diameter is stated, a taller palm stands on a stouter trunk: about 7 mm of radius a metre of greatest height (the built-in royal and date palms, 0.22 to 0.25 m at 25 to 30 m; a 3 m parlour palm about 2 cm).

generator.program.note: The lineage's own program (growth plan G2.3a), on the palm base: it gives the values its species leave unset, which the palm program gave as defaults until then.

generator.defaults.note: Values the palm program leaves to its species, near the middle of the five built-in palms' (date, royal, cabbage, saw and California fan palms), leaning to a feather palm's, since most of the family's genera are feather palms (Mabberley 2017, subfamily V Arecoideae the largest): about a dozen fronds a year, each living two or three years and opening over a year. They yield to any file's values.

growth.note: Grown to sixty years, as the built-in palms are (fifty to sixty).

variants.note: One seed in the open, as the other form defaults.

appearance.note: The built-in palms' colours and cards: a grey trunk, mid-green narrow leaflets, segments folded and drooping as the built-in fan palms' are, a green sheath for a crownshaft, a brown boot.

appearance.organs.palman.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 16): a fan leaf's unsplit middle, the palman, from which its single-fold segments part; drawn as flat wedges each twelve degrees of the fan wide (the palm program's palman_angle, so a card 0.24 as wide as long), with a few veins along it for its pleats.

appearance.organs.filament.note: Sargent (1922, p. 104): Washingtonia's segments separate on their margins into numerous slender pale fibres; drawn as fine pale threads a hundredth as wide as they are long, curling as they hang. The colour (linear [0.6, 0.55, 0.38], a pale straw) by eye.

appearance.organs.tooth.note: Dransfield et al. (2008, p. 11, 285): emergent teeth along a fan palm's petiole margins, broad at the base and pointed; drawn as triangles six tenths as wide as long, a yellow-brown (by eye) where the flora gives no colour.

appearance.leaf_axis.note: A palm's petiole and rachis are part of its leaf and coloured with it, not with the trunk: Sargent (1922) gives Thrinax floridana's petioles pale yellow-green or orange toward the base and the royal palm's green clasping bases; a yellow green, which species refine.

rules.note: What the palm program's values mean for a palm's stated characters: its frond is its whole leaf; fan or feather from its division pattern, with the petiole, its girth, rachis pieces and frond angles of the built-in fan or feather palms; suckers if it is clonal; the trunk's rise from its usual height less the crown, and its girth from its stated diameter or else its height.

traits.flower_merosity.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 241: perianth 3+3, rarely 2+2, none or many (Floral Diagrams p. 112: basic pattern trimerous).

traits.hypanthium.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 505: Simpson calls the flowers hypogynous. Simpson p. 505 defines hypogynous and epigynous as flowers without a hypanthium.

traits.note: Hutchinson (vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1959), family 393 Palmae: stems often clothed in the bases of old leaves, the leaves in a cluster at the top (scattered in climbing palms), whole or divided pinnately or palmately; flowers small and regular, in an often paniculate inflorescence among or below the leaves, with one to many spathes; perianth double, three sepals and three petals; stamens usually 6, rarely many; ovary superior, of three carpels, free or joined; fruit a berry or drupe. The stems' wood is the palms' own, with no secondary growth; they are counted woody, as the floras call them trees.

traits.leaf_habit.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Palmae: how long the leaves last (character 37), coded evergreen. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240, family Arecaceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral (rarely distichous or tristichous), usually; read as {"spiral": "usually"}.

traits.leaf_division.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240, family Arecaceae: leaf division compound (pinnate, bipinnate, costapalmate or palmate; some simple), usually; read as {"compound": "usually"}.

traits.bract_form.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240, family Arecaceae: bract form spathe, 1-many, plus large prophyll, usually; read as {"spathe": "usually"}.

traits.flowering_position.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240, family Arecaceae: flowering position lateral (infra-, inter- or suprafoliar); read as "lateral".

traits.sexual_system.note: Ingrouille, Diversity and Evolution of Land Plants (1992) p. 179, 181, family Arecaceae: sexual system monoecious, often; read as {"monoecious": "often"}. The books add hermaphrodite (sometimes): Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240: hermaphrodite.

traits.life_span.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240, family Arecaceae: life span perennial; read as "perennial".

traits.branching.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 238, 239, 240, family Arecaceae: branching unbranched (dichotomous in Hyphaene; clustered stems in some), usually. Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 478, 479, 480, family Arecaceae: branching unbranched (Corner and Holttum palms), usually. Read together as {"unbranched": "usually"}.

traits.inflorescence.note: Added kinds only; the usual kind's source is the family's `traits` note. The books add spike (sometimes): Ingrouille, Diversity and Evolution of Land Plants (1992) p. 179, 181: spike.
